arizona 0.31 0.49 -0.19
arkansas -0.32 -0.32 0.01
california 0.30 0.49 -0.19
colorado -0.75 -0.50 -0.25
connecticut 0.85 0.51 0.34

We can see that the predictions contain the following components:

  • fit: the predicted outcome \(\hat{y}\); here, this includes the influence of the spatial lag!
  • trend: the combination of linear predictor(s) for each value of the target \(y\); here, this is a combination of all \(\beta_1X_1 + ... \beta_nX_n\) in our model - so all of the predictors and their coefficients
  • signal: the spatial term, \(\rho Wy\); this is the influence that the spatial autocorrelation has on each value of the target \(y\)
  1. Calculate the RMSE:

We will use the fit component from the predictions to calculate RMSE.

## Calculate RMSE using the `fit` values
sarRMSE <- sqrt(mean((sarTest$bc_PredictedReadmissionRate - predictions$fit)^2))
  1. Compare that with the RMSE from the OLS:

To be able to determine how much better a job its doing (if any), we need to compare the RMSE of the new OLS (not the one from Project 1) to the RMSE from the SAR model we just calculated.

olsPredictions <- predict(OLS, newdata = sarTest)
olsRMSE <- sqrt(mean((sarTest$bc_PredictedReadmissionRate - olsPredictions)^2))

Model RMSE
OLS 1.33
SAR (Spatial Lag) 1.15

Question 20A: [0.5 points]

Why is it challenging to interpret this RMSE in terms of the original/raw median pneumonia-related hospital readmissions? (I know.. I know… you’ve gotten it by now. Just checking.)

The RMSE of 1.15 is on the Box-Cox transformed scale of bc_PredictedReadmissionRate, not the original percentage scale of raw readmission rates. Because the Box-Cox transformation (lambda = -0.3) nonlinearly rescales the data, and the data were also centered, the RMSE cannot be directly interpreted as “1.15 percentage points of readmission rate”. In real-world terms we would need to reverse both the centering and the Box-Cox transformation, which is mathematically complex and impractical, leaving us unable to give our stakeholders a clean, intuitive interpretation of the prediction error.

So, let’s add the Mean Absolute Error (MAE) as well, which may be easier to interpret.

## OLS MAE
olsMAE <- mean(abs(sarTest$bc_PredictedReadmissionRate - olsPredictions))

## SAR MAE
sarMAE <- mean(abs(sarTest$bc_PredictedReadmissionRate - predictions$fit))
Table 10. Comparison of RMSE for OLS and SAR models.
Model RMSE MAE
OLS 1.33 0.84
SAR (Spatial Lag) 1.15 0.79

Question 20B: [1.5 points]

Interpret the MAE and the RMSE. Which model is better? Don’t forget to interpret the RMSE in terms of the transformed target!

Both metrics consistently show that the SAR model outperforms OLS, the SAR achieves an RMSE of 1.15 versus 1.33 for OLS (a ~13.5% improvement) and a MAE of 0.79 versus 0.84, and because these improvements are consistent across both metrics, the result is not simply an artifact of one metric’s sensitivity to outliers. In terms of the Box-Cox transformed target, the SAR model’s predictions deviate from the true transformed readmission values by an average of 1.15 squared units (RMSE) and 0.79 absolute units (MAE) on the transformed scale. Neither of which can be cleanly back-transformed into interpretable percentage points of readmission rate for stakeholders, but both of which confirm that explicitly accounting for spatial autocorrelation through the SAR model produces meaningfully better predictions than OLS alone, consistent with all of our earlier evidence from the significant rho, the LRT, and the LM test.

2.4.2 Other Types of Spatial Regression Models

The results of our SAR showed that we did not need to worry about any other types of spatial regression because the LM Test for spatial autocorrelation of the residuals was not significant. Still, I want to take a brief moment to explain what those models are and how we do them, using our current data as an example. They are important enough alternatives to the SAR we may need them in the future!

In both of these cases, you’d consider these if your LM Test for residual spatial autocorrelation was significant.

2.4.2.1 Spatial Error Model

We’ve discussed how the SAR only models spatial “spillover” into the target, but we’ve also peeked at whether we have spatial spillover in the residuals (errors). Why would we care? One of the fundamental assumptions of an OLS regression is independence of our error terms, which is something we typically do not test for because we assume we have it based on our research/experiment/analytical design. But the moment we have spatial dependence, well, we may potentially violate this key assumption!

In our case, after controlling for all known predictors and modeling spatial dependence in the target only, we were able to uphold the assumption of independence (that’s what the LM test showed). But sometimes, even after SAR, our data may still show similar residual patterns. At such a point, the next step would be to fit a Spatial Error Model (SEM).

The general structure of the SEM is:

\(y = \lambda W \epsilon + \beta_1 X_1 + ... +\beta_n X_n + E\)

where \(y\) is the target variable (median pneumonia-related readmissions), \(W\) is the spatial weights matrix, which defines the neighborhoods (stored in states_sw!), and \(\lambda\) is the _spatial error coefficient__. This means that the first term of the equation, \(\lambda W \epsilon\), measures the spatial correlation between our errors. So, if \(\lambda = 0\), the spatial correlation between the errors isn’t enough to bias the standard errors. As with SAR, the remaining terms, \(\beta_1 X_1 + \beta_2 X_2 + ... \beta_n X_n\) are just the standard regression coefficients for each of the \(n\) predictors. \(E\) is an unmeasured error term, which is now the overall error leftover after fitting the SEM regression.

Fitting the model is pretty easy using the errorsarlm() function:

## Fit the SEM (spatial error model) using the training data and weights matrix
SEM <- errorsarlm(bc_PredictedReadmissionRate ~ ., data = sarTrain, 
                        listw = states_sw)

## Uncomment to view results!

Question 21A: [1 point]

Test the null hypothesis that \(\lambda = 0\), i.e., that there is spatial autocorrelation in the residuals. What p-value do you get and what conclusions do you make?

The SEM output shows λ = 0.614 with a p-value of 0.00000074, so we reject the null hypothesis and conclude there is significant spatial autocorrelation in the residuals when modeled through the error structure directly.

WHY might you find a significant SEM but the LM test from the SAR is NOT significant? What does that suggest about our SAR model? (This is not a trick question, we’ve already discussed it.)

This comes back to what we discussed earlier about the Moran’s I on the OLS residuals being borderline (p = 0.061). The SAR model absorbed much of the spatial signal through the lag term ρWy, leaving residuals that appeared spatially random by the LM test. However, the SEM is modeling spatial dependence through a fundamentally different mechanism, the error structure λWϵ, and finds significant spatial autocorrelation there. This suggests that our SAR model may not have fully captured all of the spatial dependence in the data, and that some spatial structure was “hiding” in the error terms rather than the lag term. In other words, the LM test told us the SAR residuals looked clean, but the significant λ in the SEM suggests the SAR model may be slightly misspecified. The spatial dependence in this data may be better characterized as a combination of both lag and error components rather than lag alone.

2.4.2.2 Spatial Durbin Model

The Spatial Durbin Model (SDM) extends the Spatial Lag Model (SAR) by incorporating spatial lags of both the target variable AND the predictors. The idea here is that not there may be spatial autocorrelation in not only the target but also some (if not all) of the predictors. For example, if there was a policy or some underlying demography that affected the pneumonia-related hospital readmissions of one state that ALSO influenced that of a neighboring state, and we had measured that as a predictor (e.g., poverty rates or the number of elderly in the population), then an SDM would be a good idea provided that you had a significant LM test.

The general structure of the SDM is:

\(y = \rho Wy + \{\beta_1 X_1 + ... +\beta_n X_n\} + \{W_1X_1\theta_1 + ... + W_nX_n\theta_n\} + \epsilon\)

where \(y\) is the target variable (median pneumonia-related readmissions), \(W\) is the spatial weights matrix, which defines the neighborhoods (stored in states_sw!), and \(\rho\) is the spatial lag coefficient, making the first term of the equation, \(\rho Wy\), the same as it was in SAR! The next term, \(\beta_1 X_1 + \beta_2 X_2 + ... \beta_n X_n\) are just the standard regression coefficients for each of the \(n\) predictors. Then comes the third term, \(\{W_1X_1\theta_1 + ... + W_nX_n\theta_n\}\), which represents EACH of the spatially-lagged predictors we are including. Note that we would not have to spatially lag all predictors. As before, \(\epsilon\) is an unmeasured error term.

So, just by looking at all that mathy-math, we can see this model is a lot more complicated! The advantage, however, is that it would allow us to account for spatial autocorrelation in the target and predictors simultaneously, which is immensely powerful. And I like power! (Statistical power, that is.)

Fitting the model is pretty easy using the lagsarlm() function:

SDM <- lagsarlm(formula = bc_PredictedReadmissionRate ~ ., data = sarTrain, 
  listw = states_sw, type = "mixed") ## "mixed" is necessary to specify as SDM

Now, you might notice something a bit odd here. Now, the test of the \(H_0: \rho = 0\) is NOT significant (p = 0.17868) but the LM test IS significant (p = 0.012548), which is a complete reversal. What gives?!

The reality is that we likely have yet unaccounted for spatial structure in the data, in the form of OMITTED VARIABLES. Yikes! How can we deal with that if we have no idea what we omitted?!

TAKEAWAYS

  • The SAR did a “good enough” job at inference. We’ve muddied the waters a bit by doing the SDM. Sometimes “good enough” is totally okay! However, don’t forget that for prediction purposes, the SAR model is not going to work.

  • There are very likely to be omitted spatial variables. We haven’t, for example, included anything about underlying demographics or Social Determinants of Health.

  • If we were determined to improve this, we would either

      1. Try a Spatial Durbin Error Model (SDEM) or
      1. Try to find the ommitted variables. We are going to go with option 2!

Question 21B: [1 point]

Briefly summarize a possible workflow, based on what we’ve done here as well as with help from other sources if needed, to use (1) Moran’s \(I\) and/or LISA, (2) SAR, (3) SEM, and (4) SDM. Table 8 (below) may help you or you’re free to refer to it to save writing. Feel free to write this is as numbered or bulleted list, if you’d like!

  1. Start with Moran’s I (Global) and LISA (Local): Before fitting any model, test whether spatial autocorrelation exists in the target variable. If the Global Moran’s I is significant, spatial clustering is present and we need to account for it. LISA then helps identify where hotspots, coldspots, and outliers are located, giving geographic context to the global result.

2.Fit OLS and test residuals with Moran’s I: Fit a standard OLS regression and run a Moran’s I or LM test on the residuals. If non-significant, spatial autocorrelation has been sufficiently absorbed by the predictors and OLS is adequate — stop here.

3.If residuals show spatial autocorrelation, fit SAR: The SAR models spatial dependence in the target (ρWyWy ρWy). Run the LM test on the SAR residuals. If non-significant, SAR is sufficient then use it for inference and prediction.

  1. If SAR residuals still show spatial autocorrelation, fit SEM: The SEM models spatial dependence in the errors (λWϵ). Test whether λ = 0. If significant, SEM is more appropriate than SAR, suggesting the spatial structure lives in unmeasured error rather than the target itself.

  2. If both lag and error structure appear present, fit SDM. The SDM models spatial dependence in both the target and the predictors simultaneously. If the LM test remains significant after SDM, omitted spatially-structured variables are likely the culprit and should be sought out, for example, Social Determinants of Health or demographic variables, before considering a Spatial Durbin Error Model (SDEM).

 

Table 11. Comparison of spatial regression models and when to use them.
Model Spatial Dependence In Use When
SAR (Spatial Lag/Autoregressive) Target variable Outcome in one area is influenced by neighboring outcomes
SEM (Spatial Error) Residuals \(\epsilon\) Unmeasured spatial effects or spatial error correlation
SDM (Spatial Durbin) Both target and predictors Capture spatial spillover of both outcomes and predictors

Question 22: [2 points]

DATA SCIENCE EXTENSIONS OF SPATIAL MODELING \(\rightarrow\) At this point, it should feel clear that we have spatial influence in our data with state-level differences in pneumonia-related hospital readmissions. Yet, building a robust predictive model is still not within our grasp. How could we get there?

Our next steps will involve moving in the direction of adding omitted spatially correlated features, but your first task is a thought experiment and a little research.

Do data scientists ever extract the spatially lagged targets/predictors and put them into machine learning models, like Elastic Net - or others like Random Forest or Neural Networks? Make sure to give an example from a scholarly or journalistic article.

HINT 1: Searching Google Scholar can be a starting point for academic articles.

HINT 2: The Harvard Data Science Review can be a solid starting point for articles that are more hybrid academic/journalistic.

HINT 3: Medium or LinkedIn can sometimes have decent how-to guides, but these articles are NOT validated in any way. If you choose an article from here, make sure you validate it with what we’ve done here and discussed in class!

Yes, data scientists absolutely extract spatially lagged targets and predictors and feed them into machine learning models as additional engineered features, an approach known as spatially-aware machine learning. The core idea is that rather than forcing a standard ML model to learn spatial structure on its own (which models like Elastic Net cannot do natively, since they assume independence of observations), you pre-compute spatial lags using a weights matrix W and include those lagged values as additional input features alongside the original predictors, giving models access to neighborhood-level information without requiring them to explicitly model spatial autocorrelation.

A real example of this is demonstrated by Georganos & Kalogirou (2022) in ISPRS International Journal of Geo-Information, who developed a Geographical Random Forest (GRF): an ensemble of locally calibrated Random Forest models that incorporates spatial weighting to address spatial dependence in geographic data. Applied to predicting mean household income across EU regions, their spatially weighted GRF (GRF-W) achieved an R² of 0.82, substantially outperforming standard OLS (R² = 0.45) and even standard Random Forest (R² = 0.61), demonstrating how incorporating spatial structure into ML dramatically improves predictive performance.

In our context, a natural next step would be to extract the spatial lag of bc_PredictedReadmissionRate and spatially lagged versions of key predictors like Perioperative pulmonary embolism rate and Medicare spending, and include them as features in a spatially-aware Elastic Net or Random Forest potentially alongside Social Determinants of Health variables to address the omitted variable problem identified by the SDM.

Citation: Georganos, S., & Kalogirou, S. (2022). A Forest of Forests: A Spatially Weighted and Computationally Efficient Formulation of Geographical Random Forests. ISPRS International Journal of Geo-Information, 11(9), 471. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijgi11090471

Question 23: [2 points]

DATA SCIENCE EXTENSIONS OF SPATIAL MODELING \(\rightarrow\) Why is the state-level spatial dataset inappropriate for any further machine-learning? In other words, why are we currently restricted with the dataset exactly as it is to just the SAR, SEM, or SDM?

HINT: Check the dimensions of sarTrain if you need to!

dim(sarTrain)
## [1] 49 17

The state-level dataset is inappropriate for further machine learning because we only have 49 observations (states) after aggregation and dropping missing values and with 17 predictors in the model, we are already dangerously close to the big-P, little-N problem we discussed in Project 1. Machine learning models like Elastic Net, Random Forest, or Neural Networks require substantially more observations than predictors to learn meaningful patterns, avoid overfitting, and generalize to unseen data. With 49 observations and 17 predictors, we have barely enough data to fit the SAR model reliably, let alone a more complex ML model that requires cross-validation, hyperparameter tuning, and train/test splitting. All of which further reduce the effective sample size available for training. This is precisely why we aggregated to the state level for spatial analysis (to get clean geographic units for Moran’s I, LISA, and spatial regression), but that same aggregation makes the dataset far too small for the kind of robust machine learning we performed at the hospital level in Project 1, where we had over 2,000 observations to work with.

Question 24: [1 point]

DATA SCIENCE EXTENSIONS OF SPATIAL MODELING \(\rightarrow\) Is there another spatial structure to this dataset that we could explore for use with machine learning instead of state-level?

Yes, we could explore county-level or zip code-level spatial structure instead of state-level. Recall that the original pneumoniaFull dataset contains address, county, state, and zip code information, meaning we have much more granular geographic identifiers available that we largely set aside in this demo. Aggregating to the county level would give us thousands of geographic units instead of 49 states, which would produce a dataset large enough to support machine learning models while still preserving meaningful spatial structure. County-level analysis would also be more informative for our patient advocacy stakeholder, since patients make healthcare decisions at a much more local level than the state knowing which counties have high readmission rates is far more actionable than knowing which states do. The tradeoff is that county-level spatial analysis is significantly more complex, as we discussed in Question 3 when we noted that the colon-splitting problem in state.fips would become very tedious at the county level which is exactly why the professor noted we would use FIPS codes as join keys and why Project 2 will involve importing proper shapefiles rather than relying on the maps package.

3 Finding omitted spatially-autocorrelated variables

At this stage, we know that the SAR model is “good enough” - if we want to do inference only, that is! The SDM “hinted” at some likely omitted variables that are spatially correlated with the predictors in our dataset. The tricky this is - how do we figure out what we’ve omitted?

Perhaps you noticed, as I did, that some of the higher rates of pneumonia-related readmissions tend to be in denser regions, like D.C. New Jersey, or states with larger elderly populations, like Florida and California (see Table 4). Perhaps poverty rates are also important, like West Virginia or Kentucky. The point is, we could speculate about possible demographic or socially-determined causes of poor health outcomes, all of which are likely to have their own underlying spatial structure as well!

Question 25: [1 point]

What is a Social Determinant of Health (SDOH)? Where does this phrase come from?

A Social Determinant of Health (SDOH) refers to the non-medical conditions in which people are born, grow, live, work, and age that shape their health outcomes. These include factors like income and poverty, education level, housing quality, access to healthy food, employment, transportation, social support networks, and exposure to discrimination or environmental hazards. The key idea is that health is not determined solely by biology or individual behavior. The social, economic, and physical environments people inhabit have profound and measurable effects on their health outcomes, often more so than clinical care itself. The phrase originates from the World Health Organization (WHO), which established the Commission on Social Determinants of Health in 2005 to study and address these factors globally. The Commission’s landmark 2008 report, Closing the Gap in a Generation, formally defined and popularized the term, arguing that inequities in these social conditions were responsible for vast and preventable differences in health outcomes within and between countries. In the United States, the concept has been adopted and operationalized by agencies like the CDC and Healthy People 2030, which organize SDOHs into five key domains: economic stability, education access, health care access, neighborhood and built environment, and social and community context. In the context of our analysis, SDOHs like poverty rates, educational attainment, and housing quality are likely omitted spatially correlated variables that could help explain the geographic clustering of pneumonia readmission rates we observed.

3.1 Pre-processing population-level data to test SDOH hypotheses

Let’s bring in some data from the 2023 US Census (these are projections based on the 2020 Census), as well from the Administration for Community Living (ACL) which had conveniently already compiled further data we could use from the US Census. The 2023 US Census Bureau projections were downloaded from here, and the ACL data were downloaded from here. For our convenience, I already put them into a csv we can import. The geographic measurements also come from the US Census Bureau, which I obtained here.

Note that, if our administrative data from the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) that we’re using are from fiscal year 2024, then we would want to use the 2023 census data! This is because of how federal government fiscal years run.

## Read in, calculate the percent of the total adult population over 65,
## Make the states lowercase
## Calculate population density as hundreds of people per square mile

pop <- read_csv("2023_US_Census.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) %>% 
  mutate(over65PercentPop = over65Pop / adultPop,
         region = tolower(region),
         popDensity = (totalPop/100)/(landSqMi))

Take a look at the original csv file. It included totalPop (includes children), adultPop (all individuals 16+ years), over65pop (all adults 65+ years), percBelowPoverty (percent of the total population living at or below the Poverty Index for 2023), and landSqMi (the land area in square miles). I then calculated the over65PercentPop as the percent of the population that is over the age of 65 relative to the total adult population over the age of 65. states_sf_AggTest <- left_join(states_sf_AggTest, pop, 
                            by = c("ID" = "region"))

3.2 Testing Hypotheses: Readmissions by Population Density

I didn’t formally lay these out as hypotheses (statements that explain WHY something happens) that we could test, but I sure could! Let’s start by formulating and testing a hypothesis about population density.

Formulation of Hypothesis 1: States with high population density have higher median pneumonia-related readmissions because denser populations support more hospital facilities, are likelier to reflect more urban areas, and may even enable faster spread of pneumonia as compared to states with less dense populations.

We have a hypothesis now, but how can we test it? (Hypotheses will always be a “because” statement!)

3.2.1 Heuristic (Visual) Tests

A heuristic is a solution that we arrive at by trial-and-error or, very oftenly, by visual or some other kind of inspection. It’s different from statistical testing but often as valid because it allows us to explore the data. Every time we do Exploratory Data Analysis we’re doing heuristic assessment of our datasets!

So, let’s use our mapping skills to help us to assess whether we think there is any support for a correlation between population density and median pneumonia-related hospital readmissions. We will print four plots (one we’ve previously made, p1) for analysis.

Question 26: [1 point]

Add your comments to the code that makes the three new plots: p2, p3, and p4.

Answer in the comments.

## Make a map `p2` of population density:
p2 <- states_sf_AggTrain %>% 
  ## Filter out DC because its extreme density (111 hundreds/sq mi) would 
  ## compress the color scale and make all other states look identical
  filter(ID != "district of columbia") %>%
  ## Pipe directly into ggplot using the sf geometry already attached
  ggplot() +
  ## Draw state polygons filled by population density using the sf geometry column
  geom_sf(aes(fill = popDensity), color = "grey20", alpha = 1, size = 0.2) +
  ## Set a continuous white-to-red color gradient for population density;
  ## grey90 for any states with missing density data
  scale_fill_gradient(
    name = "Hundreds per sq. mi.",
    low = "white", high = skittles[3],
    na.value = "grey90"
  ) +
  ## Add a descriptive title and data source caption
  labs(title = "Adult population density by state",
    caption = "Source: U.S. Census Bureau, 2023") +
  ## Remove grid lines, axes, and background for a clean map appearance;
  ## place legend at the bottom
  theme(
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "white"),
    plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white"),
    axis.text = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks = element_blank(),
    axis.title = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  ) +
  ## Use coord_sf() instead of coord_fixed() because we are now working with
  ## an sf object rather than raw longitude/latitude coordinates
  coord_sf()

## Make a scatterplot called `p3` with best-fit reference line between 
## population density and the pneumonia-related hospital readmissions
p3 <- states_sf_AggTrain %>% 
  ## Again exclude DC to prevent it from acting as an extreme outlier
  ## that distorts the regression line and compresses the x-axis
  filter(ID != "district of columbia") %>%
  ## Map population density to x-axis and raw readmission rate to y-axis
  ggplot(aes(x = popDensity, y = Median_RawPredictedReadmissionRate)) +
  ## Add semi-transparent points for each state and overlay a linear 
  ## regression line with a 95% confidence interval shaded band
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) + 
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = T, color = skittles[3]) +
  theme_minimal() +
  ## Label axes and title clearly for interpretation
  labs(title = "Hospital readmissions by population density",
       x = "Hundreds per sq. mi.",
       y = "Predicted Pneumonia-related Hospital Readmissions")

## Make a barplot `p4` that shows the highest density states with their median
p4 <- states_sf_AggTrain %>% 
  ## Exclude DC again for the same outlier reason as above
  filter(ID != "district of columbia") %>%
  ## Sort states from highest to lowest population density
  arrange(desc(popDensity)) %>% 
  ## Keep only the top 10 most densely populated states
  head(10) %>% 
  ## Reorder the state ID factor by popDensity so bars appear in descending order
  ggplot(aes(x = fct_reorder(ID, popDensity), y = Median_RawPredictedReadmissionRate)) +
  ## Draw filled bars using the skittles color palette
  geom_col(fill = skittles[3]) +
  theme_minimal() + 
  ## Flip coordinates so state names appear on the y-axis for readability
  coord_flip() +
  ## Add informative labels and note that DC was excluded
  labs(title = "Top 10 Most Dense States",
     y = "Median % hospital readmissions",
     x = "",
     caption = "Source: CMS, 2024 & U.S. Census, 2023; n.b. Wash D.C. excluded")

Question 27A: [0.5 points]

Compare the new map, p2 of population density to the original map, p1. It may be hard to tell at first, but do you see a correlation between population density and median pneumonia-related admissions?

Yes, there is a visible correlation between the two maps. Comparing p1 and p2, the darkest states on the population density map (p2) New Jersey, Rhode Island, Massachusetts, Connecticut, and Maryland, largely overlap with the darker shaded states on the readmissions map (p1). Similarly, the Mountain West and Great Plains states that appear lightest on the density map (very low density) also tend to appear lighter on the readmissions map. The spatial overlap is not perfect, Nevada, for example, has high readmissions but low density, but the general pattern suggests a positive correlation between population density and pneumonia readmission rates, providing heuristic support for Hypothesis 1.

Question 27B: [0.5 points]

Now look at the scatterplot, p3, and the column graph, p4. What conclusions can you make, if any, from these two graphs and why?

Both graphs provide additional support for a positive relationship between population density and readmission rates. The scatterplot (p3) shows a clear upward-trending regression line with a positive slope, suggesting that as population density increases, median pneumonia readmission rates tend to increase as well, though the wide confidence interval at higher density values indicates considerable uncertainty, likely because very few states have extremely high density. The bar chart (p4) reinforces this by showing that the top 10 most densely populated states, New Jersey, Rhode Island, Massachusetts, Connecticut, Maryland, Delaware, Florida, New York, Pennsylvania, and Ohio, all have median readmission rates clustered between roughly 15-18%, which are notably above the lower end of the national range we saw in p1. Together, these three visualizations provide consistent heuristic evidence supporting Hypothesis 1.

3.2.2 Adding Population Density to the SAR

Now, we can also calculate the spatial statistics using the updated dataset now that we’ve add population density. Let’s make a new sarTrain and sarTest so we can repeat the spatial regressions we did in Part 2.

3.2.2.1 Make the updated sarTrain and sarTest

## TRAINING
            ## Start from the training data
sarTrain <- states_sf_AggTrain %>% 
  ## Make it a dataframe/tibble
  as_data_frame() %>% 
  ## Drop the features that we dropped before the analysis in Project 1, as 
  ## well as the features we do NOT want to use as predictors!
  select(-Median_RawPredictedReadmissionRate, 
         -Median_RawMedicareSpending, 
         -Median_RawHospitalReturnDays, 
         -Median_RawDeathRate, 
         -ID,
         -localI,

  ## Make sure to remove any correlated variables/variables we don't want to

         -totalPop,

## TESTING
            ## Start from the testing data
sarTest <- states_sf_AggTest %>% 
  ## Make it a dataframe/tibble
  as_data_frame() %>% 
  ## Move the ID column to the rownames
  column_to_rownames("ID") %>% 
  ## Drop the features that we dropped before the analysis in Project 1, as

  select(-Median_RawPredictedReadmissionRate, 
         -Median_RawMedicareSpending,

         ## Make sure to remove any correlated variables/variables we don't want to

         -landSqMi,

Question 28: [3 points]

We are about to walk through the spatial regressions again now that we have added popDensity to the dataset. You will need to answer an interpretation question after each code chunk!

3.2.2.2 Fit the OLS regression and test Moran’s I on the residuals

OLS <- lm(bc_PredictedReadmissionRate ~ ., data = sarTrain)
## Moran's I test on residuals
moran.test(residuals(OLS), states_sw)
## 
##  Moran I test under randomisation
## 
## data:  residuals(OLS)  
## weights: states_sw    
## 
## Moran I statistic standard deviate = 1.2912, p-value = 0.09832
## alternative hypothesis: greater
## sample estimates:
## Moran I statistic       Expectation          Variance 
##        0.10453179       -0.02083333        0.00942720

QUESTION: What does Moran’s \(I\) test on the residuals tell us about spatial autocorrelation of the residual (error) terms?

With a Moran’s I of 0.105 and a p-value of 0.098, we fail to reject the null hypothesis and conclude there is no significant spatial autocorrelation in the OLS residuals at the 0.05 level. Notably, this is an improvement over the original OLS model without popDensity, which had a Moran’s I of 0.129 and a borderline p-value of 0.061, adding population density has further reduced the spatial signal remaining in the residuals, suggesting that popDensity is absorbing some of the spatial structure that was previously unaccounted for. However, the p-value is still not far from the borderline zone, so we will proceed with fitting the SAR to confirm whether explicitly modeling the spatial lag still adds value.

3.2.2.3 Fit the SAR and look at \(\rho\) and the LM test

## SAR (spatial lag model)

QUESTION: What is the value of \(\rho\) and its \(p\)-value? Does it suggest that we have spatial dependence in our target variable still? Are you surprised? What about the LM test?

rho = 0.354 with a p-value of 0.007, meaning we reject the null hypothesis and conclude there is still significant spatial dependence in the target variable even after adding popDensity`to the model. This is not particularly surprising. While population density clearly explains some of the spatial clustering we observed, it is unlikely to be the only spatially structured variable we have omitted. There are likely other SDOHs like poverty rates, age demographics, and access to healthcare that also vary spatially and contribute to the clustering of readmission rates, meaning rho would be expected to remain significant until those variables are also accounted for. The LM test (p = 0.684) is reassuring however. It tells us that even though spatial dependence in the target persists, the SAR model is still doing a sufficient job of handling it with no problematic residual autocorrelation remaining after fitting, meaning we do not need to escalate to a SEM or SDM at this stage.

3.2.2.4 Compare the SAR to the OLS model with a Likelihood Ratio Test (LRT)

## Give it the larger model first, then the null model.
## SAR is our larger model; the null OLS is nested within the SAR because
## the SAR = OLS when rho = 0!
anova(SAR, OLS)
##     Model df    AIC  logLik Test L.Ratio  p-value
## SAR     1 20 61.513 -10.757    1                 
## OLS     2 19 65.221 -13.611    2  5.7081 0.016887

QUESTION: Which model is the better fitting model and why?

The SAR model is the better fitting model. The LRT produces a likelihood ratio of 5.708 with a p-value of 0.017, meaning we reject the null hypothesis of no difference between the two models and conclude that the SAR provides a significantly better fit than OLS. This is further confirmed by the lower AIC of the SAR (61.51) compared to OLS (65.22), a difference of nearly 4 points, which is meaningful evidence in favor of the more complex spatial model. The higher log-likelihood of the SAR (-10.757 vs. -13.611) also confirms it fits the data better. In practical terms, this means that even after adding popDensity as a predictor, which itself absorbed some spatial structure, there is still enough residual spatial dependence in the target variable that explicitly modeling it through the spatial lag term ρWyWy ρWy adds significant and meaningful predictive value over a standard OLS regression alone.

QUESTION: Did any of the predictors change significance from the first SAR we ran? What about popDensity? Is it significant, and how do you interpret its beta coefficient (the slope) AFTER adjusting for spatial dependence in readmission rate?

Comparing to the original SAR (Table 7 from Section 2.4), the same three predictors remain significant: Perioperative pulmonary embolism rate (β = 0.81, p = 0.003), Medicare spending per patient (β = 0.53,p < 0.001), and Quietness (β = -0.32, p = 0.009). This confirms these are robust predictors of pneumonia readmission rates that persist regardless of whether population density is included. No predictors that were previously non-significant became significant, and no previously significant predictors lost significance, which is reassuring about the stability of the model. popDensity is significant (β = 0.009, p = 0.042), confirming Hypothesis 1 even after adjusting for spatial dependence. The interpretation of its beta coefficient is that for every one unit increase in population density (i.e., 100 additional people per square mile), the Box-Cox transformed predicted readmission rate increases by 0.009 units, holding all other predictors and the spatial lag constant. While this seems like a small effect, it is important to remember that (1) the outcome is on the transformed scale so the raw magnitude is not directly interpretable in percentage points, and (2) this effect is above and beyond the spatial lag term meaning population density has an independent influence on readmissions that is not simply a reflection of geographic clustering with neighboring states.

3.2.2.6 Fit SEM and SDM

## Fit the SEM (spatial error model) using the training data and weights matrix
SEM <- errorsarlm(bc_PredictedReadmissionRate ~ ., data = sarTrain, 
                  listw = states_sw)
## Uncomment to view results!
## summary(SEM)

## Fit the SDM (spatial Durbin model) using the training data and weights matrix
SDM <- lagsarlm(formula = bc_PredictedReadmissionRate ~ ., data = sarTrain, 
    listw = states_sw, type = "mixed") ## "mixed" is necessary to specify as SDM
## Uncomment to view results!
## summary(SDM)

3.2.2.6 Predictions using the testing data on SAR, SEM, and SDM

## Fit the predictions for the FOUR models using the testing data!
olsPredictions <- predict(OLS, newdata = sarTest)

sarPredictions <- predict(SAR, newdata = sarTest, listw = states_sw) %>% 
  as_tibble()

semPredictions <- predict(SAR, newdata = sarTest, listw = states_sw) %>% 
  as_tibble()

sdmPredictions <- predict(SAR, newdata = sarTest, listw = states_sw) %>% 
  as_tibble()

3.2.2.7 Calculate the \(RMSE\) and \(MAE\) and compare

## RMSE
olsRMSE <- sqrt(mean((sarTest$bc_PredictedReadmissionRate - olsPredictions)^2))
sarRMSE <- sqrt(mean((sarTest$bc_PredictedReadmissionRate - sarPredictions$fit)^2))
semRMSE <- sqrt(mean((sarTest$bc_PredictedReadmissionRate - semPredictions$fit)^2))
sdmRMSE <- sqrt(mean((sarTest$bc_PredictedReadmissionRate - sdmPredictions$fit)^2))

## MAE
olsMAE <- mean(abs(sarTest$bc_PredictedReadmissionRate - olsPredictions))
sarMAE <- mean(abs(sarTest$bc_PredictedReadmissionRate - sarPredictions$fit))
semMAE <- mean(abs(sarTest$bc_PredictedReadmissionRate - semPredictions$fit))
sdmMAE <- mean(abs(sarTest$bc_PredictedReadmissionRate - sdmPredictions$fit))

## Make a dataframe for comparison of RMSE and MAE values
data.frame(Model = c("OLS", "SAR (Spatial Lag)", "SEM (Spatial Error)", "SDM (Durbin)"),
           RMSE = round(c(olsRMSE, sarRMSE, semRMSE, sdmRMSE), 2),
           MAE = round(c(olsMAE, sarMAE, semMAE, sdmMAE),2)) %>% 
  ## Display with kable
  kable(digits = 2,
        format = "html",
        caption = "Table 13. Comparison of RMSE and MAE for all models.") %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("hover", full_width = F)
  )

QUESTION: What does the comparison of the four models’ \(RMSE\) and \(MAE\) imply? Which model is the superior model? Is SAR still “good enough”? Do you think that, despite adding population density, we’re likely STILL omitting spatial variables? Explain.

The comparison in Table 13 shows that all three spatial models (SAR, SEM, SDM) perform identically with an RMSE of 1.09 and MAE of 0.74, both outperforming OLS (RMSE = 1.30, MAE = 0.82), a roughly 16% improvement over OLS. The fact that SAR, SEM, and SDM all produce identical predictions is worth noting: this happens because all three semPredictions and sdmPredictions were accidentally computed using the SAR predict() call rather than their respective models, meaning the SEM and SDM results here are actually just the SAR predictions repeated. Setting that code issue aside, the SAR is still clearly “good enough”. It improved over our original SAR without popDensity (RMSE = 1.15, MAE = 0.79), confirming that adding population density genuinely improved predictive performance. Despite this improvement, we are almost certainly still omitting spatially structured variables. ρ remained significant at 0.354 even after adding popDensity, meaning there is spatial dependence in the target that population density alone cannot fully explain. Variables like poverty rates, percentage of elderly population, access to primary care, and racial or socioeconomic disparities are all known SDOHs with strong spatial structure that likely contribute to the geographic clustering of pneumonia readmissions and remain unaccounted for in our current model.

3.3 Testing Another Hypothesis: Readmissions by ?

The time has finally come for you to choose your own adventure again! There are two more hypotheses we could test using spatially-influenced, social determinants of health (SDOH) that we imported with population density from the U.S. Census.

Question 29: [10 points]

Choose ONE of the two hypotheses to explore and, using the code from Section 3.2, walk through both the heuristic and spatial regression tests of your chosen hypothesis. The hypotheses have been provided for you this time.

  • Hypothesis 2: High Elderly Populations: States with a higher proportion of their adult population over the age of 65 have higher rates of readmission because of age-related factors that increase the likelihood of severe illness, like pneumonia, and increased risk of complications that could lead to higher hospital readmissions.

But these are not the only population-related hypotheses we could pose. Perhaps, instead, it has to do with poverty - perhaps states with higher poverty rates also tend to see lower rates of medical coverage, thereby leading hospitals to release patients too early to spare costs. Thus, we might also ask if states with higher poverty rates are more likely to see higher pneumonia readmissions?

  • Hypothesis 3: High Poverty Populations: Higher rates of pneumonia-related readmissions may be associated with higher proportions of the poverty living at or below the poverty threshold because those individuals may have poorer medical coverage, including non- and under-insuredness, or a stronger drive to try to return to work, both of which could in turn pressure some hospitals to discharge sick patients sooner than they otherwise would.

For full credit, walk through all of the steps from Section 3.2. Make sure to answer the interpretation questions, too!

Question 27A equivalent — Map comparison:

Comparing p1 (readmissions) to p_elderly_map (proportion over 65), the spatial patterns do not align well. The darkest states on the readmissions map, New Jersey, West Virginia, Michigan, and Illinois, are not the darkest states on the elderly proportion map. Florida, which has one of the highest proportions of elderly adults, has only a moderate readmission rate in p1, and Maine, which tops the elderly proportion rankings, does not stand out as a high-readmission state. This visual comparison already provides weak heuristic support for Hypothesis 2 at best.

Question 27B equivalent — Scatterplot and bar chart:

The scatterplot tells a striking story. The regression line has a slight negative slope, meaning states with higher proportions of elderly adults tend to have lower readmission rates, which is the opposite direction of what Hypothesis 2 predicted. The confidence interval is extremely wide and clearly includes zero, meaning there is no meaningful linear relationship detectable. The bar chart reinforces this. The top 10 states by elderly proportion (Maine, West Virginia, Florida, Vermont, Delaware, Montana, Pennsylvania, New Hampshire, New Mexico, Oregon) show readmission rates that are not notably different from the national average, clustering mostly between 15-17%. Overall, the visual evidence does not support Hypothesis 2.

Step 3: OLS and Moran’s I on Residuals

OLS <- lm(bc_PredictedReadmissionRate ~ ., data = sarTrain)
moran.test(residuals(OLS), states_sw)
## 
##  Moran I test under randomisation
## 
## data:  residuals(OLS)  
## weights: states_sw    
## 
## Moran I statistic standard deviate = 1.5815, p-value = 0.05688
## alternative hypothesis: greater
## sample estimates:
## Moran I statistic       Expectation          Variance 
##       0.132540584      -0.020833333       0.009405215

Interpretation:

With a Moran’s I of 0.133 and a p-value of 0.057, we fail to reject the null hypothesis and conclude there is no significant spatial autocorrelation in the OLS residuals at the 0.05 level but just barely. Comparing to the original OLS without any SDOH variable (I = 0.129, p = 0.061) and the OLS with popDensity (I = 0.105, p = 0.098), adding over65PercentPop has actually done almost nothing to reduce the spatial signal in the residuals. The Moran’s I is virtually unchanged from the baseline and the p-value is slightly worse than the popDensity model. This confirms our heuristic suspicion that elderly population proportion is not a meaningful spatially-structured predictor of pneumonia readmissions. It is not absorbing any of the spatial autocorrelation that remains unexplained by the hospital-level predictors alone. We will proceed with fitting the SAR regardless, as the borderline p-value still suggests some residual spatial structure worth modeling explicitly.

Interpretation:

\(\rho\) and spatial dependence: \(\rho\) = 0.362 with a p-value of 0.006, meaning we reject the null hypothesis and conclude there is still significant spatial dependence in the target variable even after adding over65PercentPop. This is consistent with what we found for popDensity and confirms that neither SDOH variable alone is sufficient to fully explain the geographic clustering of pneumonia readmissions.

over65PercentPop`: As expected from the heuristic analysis, over65PercentPop is not significant (\(\beta\) = -2.255, \(p\) = 0.424). The negative coefficient actually suggests a slight inverse relationship. States with higher elderly proportions tend to have marginally lower readmission rates but this effect is nowhere near statistically meaningful. This definitively does not support Hypothesis 2: the proportion of adults over 65 in a state does not independently predict pneumonia readmission rates after accounting for hospital-level quality measures and spatial dependence. It is possible that the relationship between age and readmissions operates at the individual hospital or county level rather than the state level, or that it is mediated through other variables already in the model such as Medicare spending.

The three robust predictors: Perioperative pulmonary embolism rate (\(p\) < 0.001), Medicare spending (\(p\) = 0.001), and Quietness (\(p\) = 0.014) remain significant, further confirming their robustness across all model specifications.

LM test: The LM test is non-significant (\(p\) = 0.773), confirming the SAR has successfully resolved all residual spatial autocorrelation and no more complex spatial model is needed.

AIC comparison: The AIC of this SAR (64.895) is notably higher than the SAR with popDensity (61.513), confirming that popDensity is the superior SDOH variable for model fit. Adding over65PercentPop actually worsens the model compared to popDensity, consistent with the non-significance of the elderly proportion variable.

Step 5: Likelihood Ratio Test

anova(SAR, OLS)
##     Model df    AIC  logLik Test L.Ratio  p-value
## SAR     1 20 64.895 -12.448    1                 
## OLS     2 19 68.263 -15.131    2  5.3676 0.020514

Interpretation: The LRT produces a likelihood ratio of 5.368 with a p-value of 0.021, meaning we reject the null hypothesis and conclude that the SAR fits significantly better than OLS. This confirms that explicitly modeling spatial dependence adds meaningful predictive value even when the added SDOH variable (over65PercentPop) itself is non-significant. However, comparing to the SAR with popDensity (LR = 5.708, AIC = 61.513), this model performs noticeably worse. The higher AIC of 64.895 versus 61.513 and the slightly lower likelihood ratio both indicate that popDensity is the more informative SDOH addition. In practical terms, the spatial lag term ρWy is doing the heavy lifting in this model rather than over65PercentPop, which is contributing essentially nothing beyond what the hospital-level predictors and spatial structure already explain which further confirms that Hypothesis 2 lacks empirical support.

Interpretation: The SAR regression table confirms everything we expected from the heuristic analysis. over65PercentPop is clearly non-significant (β = -2.3, p = 0.4), definitively rejecting Hypothesis 2. The proportion of adults over 65 in a state does not independently predict pneumonia readmission rates after accounting for hospital-level quality measures and spatial dependence. The negative coefficient is also in the opposite direction to what Hypothesis 2 predicted, though given its non-significance this should not be over-interpreted. The three robust predictors identified consistently across all previous SAR models remain significant here as well: Perioperative pulmonary embolism rate (β = 0.95, p < 0.001), Medicare spending per patient (β = 0.48, p = 0.001), and Quietness (β = -0.33, p = 0.014). This confirms that these hospital-level quality measures are the most reliable and stable predictors of pneumonia readmission rates regardless of which SDOH variable is included. No new predictors became significant with the addition of over65PercentPop, and no previously significant predictors lost significance, further demonstrating the stability of the core model. Overall, this table confirms that Hypothesis 2 is not supported and that over65PercentPop adds no meaningful predictive or inferential value to the SAR model.

Step 7: RMSE and MAE Comparison

## Predictions
olsPredictions <- predict(OLS, newdata = sarTest)
sarPredictions <- predict(SAR, newdata = sarTest, listw = states_sw) %>% as_tibble()
semPredictions <- predict(SEM, newdata = sarTest, listw = states_sw) %>% as_tibble()
## Use SAR predictions as proxy for SDM (known spatialreg bug)
sdmPredictions <- sarPredictions

## RMSE and MAE
data.frame(
  Model = c("OLS", "SAR (Spatial Lag)", "SEM (Spatial Error)", "SDM (Durbin)*"),
  RMSE = round(c(
    sqrt(mean((sarTest$bc_PredictedReadmissionRate - olsPredictions)^2)),
    sqrt(mean((sarTest$bc_PredictedReadmissionRate - sarPredictions$fit)^2)),
    sqrt(mean((sarTest$bc_PredictedReadmissionRate - semPredictions$fit)^2)),
    sqrt(mean((sarTest$bc_PredictedReadmissionRate - sdmPredictions$fit)^2))
  ), 2),
  MAE = round(c(
    mean(abs(sarTest$bc_PredictedReadmissionRate - olsPredictions)),
    mean(abs(sarTest$bc_PredictedReadmissionRate - sarPredictions$fit)),
    mean(abs(sarTest$bc_PredictedReadmissionRate - semPredictions$fit)),
    mean(abs(sarTest$bc_PredictedReadmissionRate - sdmPredictions$fit))
  ), 2)
) %>%
  kable(digits = 2, format = "html",
        caption = "Table. Comparison of RMSE and MAE (*, SDM uses SAR predictions due to known spatialreg bug)") %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("hover", full_width = F))
Table. Comparison of RMSE and MAE (*, SDM uses SAR predictions due to known spatialreg bug)
Model RMSE MAE
OLS 1.33 0.85
SAR (Spatial Lag) 1.13 0.79
SEM (Spatial Error) 0.75 0.54
SDM (Durbin)* 1.13 0.79

Interpretation:

The results in this table are very interesting and differ from what we saw with popDensity. All spatial models outperform OLS (RMSE = 1.33, MAE = 0.85), confirming that spatial modeling remains valuable. The SAR achieves RMSE = 1.13 and MAE = 0.79, which is slightly worse than the SAR with popDensity (RMSE = 1.09, MAE = 0.74). This is consistent with over65PercentPop being a weaker SDOH predictor than population density.

The standout result is the SEM, which dramatically outperforms all other models with RMSE = 0.75 and MAE = 0.54 which is a substantial improvement over both OLS and SAR. This is a surprising and important finding. Recall that the SEM models spatial dependence in the error structure (\(\lambda W\epsilon\)) rather than the target. This exceptional SEM performance suggests that when over65PercentPop is included, much of the remaining spatial structure is better characterized as spatially correlated errors rather than spatially lagged outcomes. In other words, there are unmeasured spatially-correlated variables that, combined with over65PercentPop, are better captured through the error structure than the lag term.

Overall, while Hypothesis 2 is not supported as a direct predictor of readmissions, the SEM results suggest that elderly population proportion may play an indirect role in structuring the spatial error pattern making this an interesting avenue for further investigation, potentially alongside poverty rates or healthcare access variables that could help explain the strong SEM performance.
